ai.chatQ: Why is my runway shorter than I calculated?

problem.leadMuted: The language people use for it was made that way.

s1.title: Words instead of meaning
s1.body: Diversification, liquidity, multiples. Behind each one sits a simple idea nobody bothers to translate back into plain speech.

s2.title: Advice without context
s2.body: “Just buy the index” is good advice for one person and bad for another. The difference is rarely explained, and the difference is everything.

s3.title: No practice
s3.body: Reading about risk and feeling it are different things. The first takes an evening; the second usually costs money.

problem.answer: Zinvest runs the other way round: you make the decision first, then work out where it leads.
problem.answer2: Every term shows up the minute you actually need it — not in the third paragraph of a chapter you never reached.

demo.title: You have $10,000. What would you do?
demo.lede: There is no right answer — only consequences. Pick one and see where it lands ten years out.

invest.label: Invest
invest.hint: A broad index fund, then leave it alone.
invest.after: in {years} years, if the market behaved as it usually does
invest.says: That growth isn't a gift; it is the fee for sitting through the drops. Over ten years this would have fallen 20–30% twice, and the real question isn't the final number — it's whether you'd sell at the bottom.

save.label: Save
save.hint: A savings account, money within reach.
save.says: The money is still there, and that matters: you can take it out tomorrow. But inflation works all ten of those years too, so the question isn't the figure on screen — it's what that figure will buy.

spend.label: Spend
spend.hint: Now, on what is needed now.
spend.after: in {years} years — the money is spent
spend.says: This isn't a mistake by itself. Clearing debt at 20%, or finally having an emergency fund, is often the best thing this money can do. The mistake is spending it without knowing what you gave up.

demo.forgone: Difference against the best of the three: {amount}.
demo.assumption: Assumes 7% a year for the index and 4% for the account. Before tax and inflation.

ai.q: Why buy an ETF instead of individual stocks?
ai.a: One ETF is a basket of hundreds of companies at once. If one of them fails, you lose its slice rather than your stake. You aren't buying the best company — you're buying the whole market, and its average growth with it.
ai.a_simpler: Picture a tray of eggs. A single stock is one egg: drop it and there's no breakfast. An ETF is the whole tray — one breaks, the rest are fine.
ai.a_example: $1,000 in one airline's stock in early 2020 would have been about $400 two months later. The same $1,000 in a broad index would have been about $700 — and back above where it started by the end of the year.
ai.a_quiz: Good. You own an ETF of the 500 largest companies and one of them goes bankrupt. What happens to your money?
ai.quizOpt1: I lose everything I put in
ai.quizRight: Yes. Its weight in the index is a fraction of a percent, and the fund simply replaces it with the next company.
ai.quizWrong: Not quite: the stake is spread across 500 companies, so any one of them is a fraction of a percent, not the whole thing.

q1.q: You've just got your stipend. What's the smartest first move?
q1.a1: Spend it on something you've wanted for ages
q1.a2: Put part of it into an emergency fund
q1.a3: Lend it to a friend — they'll pay it back
q1.why: An emergency fund is money for the unexpected: a broken phone, getting ill. Set part aside first, then spend the rest with a clear head.

q2.q: A phone costs 3,000,000 sum. On instalments it's 12 payments of 300,000 sum. How much extra do you pay?
q2.why: 12 × 300,000 = 3,600,000 sum — 600,000 more than the price. That's what the “convenience” of instalments costs.

q3.a1: Prices rise, so the same money buys less
q3.a2: The interest a bank pays on your savings
q3.a3: A tax you pay on every purchase
q3.why: If prices rise 10% in a year, a year from now 100,000 sum buys what costs about 91,000 today.
